input.question: I don't have a gym—what can I do at home or with everyday items to stay active?
input.story:
Last Monday, I had to carry boxes of textbooks from the staffroom to my class. Sounds simple, yes? I thought so too. After only three trips, my arms felt weak, sweat was dripping down my face, and my legs wobbled like soft ugali. I sat on a bench, embarrassed, while the headteacher looked at me. Was it just the heat, or was my body telling me to wake up? Maybe I have been ignoring my health for too long, but surely, I just need more rest?

The very next day, the local clinic nurse, Sister Participant, visited our school for health talks. She saw me limping up the steps. She asked, 'Participant, are you caring for your diabetes?' I gave a small laugh and said gyms are for towns, not here. She smiled and replied, 'You don’t need a gym. Use what you have—buckets, chairs, even walking to school. Ten minutes, two or three times a day.' She showed me how to march in place as I waited for water to boil, and how sweeping the compound could be real exercise too. That sounded too easy, or maybe too hopeful. Still, could moving a little make such a big difference?

At first, I felt awkward, like a goat escaping a line. While waiting for tea, I lifted a bucket over my head, only for the lid to fall off and water to splash on my skirt. I nearly stopped, but I remembered that this Friday, all teachers must rearrange the heavy desks for class repairs. Would I faint in front of my pupils again? No! So, each day, I marched and stretched while cooking, swept extra hard, and walked to friends’ homes instead of calling them over. The changes felt strange, and I missed the old rhythm, but I tried slowing my breath, just like Sister Participant said.

By Friday, when we pushed those desks, my shirt clung to my back, but I was standing strong. I finished my share, laughed with the others, and didn’t need to run for the bench. My legs still shook, but not from weakness—maybe just pride. That night, I even taught my favourite ajua game under the big mango tree, showing the children silly exercise steps with each move. Who would have guessed that a bucket and a short walk could make me feel proud? Maybe I won’t stop here, not anymore.

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
I’m Participant, and I wake up early like every day, before the sun is high. I go to my farm, feed the goats, and plant maize. I work till midday, then go back to the house to cook. I eat my meals at the right time—breakfast, lunch, dinner. But sometimes, when the sun goes down, I feel tired. My body is weak, and I just want something to eat. So I eat a piece of bread with a bit of milk. I don’t think about it much—just ‘I’m hungry, so I eat’. But I wonder… if I eat late at night, will my body get sick? Will my sugar go up? I don’t know. I just eat. And last week, I forgot to check my blood sugar after eating late. My son said I looked tired and my hands were shaky. I thought, ‘Oh, it’s just tiredness’. But then I saw the nurse at the clinic, and she said, ‘Participant, your sugar is high’. I didn’t understand. I just said, ‘I didn’t mean to eat late’. But she said, ‘You did. And that’s dangerous’. I felt bad. I didn’t know it could hurt me. That night, I tried to stop, but I was too tired. The next day, I went to the farm again, and I forgot to take my insulin. I felt weak. I just wanted to rest. I didn’t know what to do. That’s when I thought—maybe I need to change how I eat, not just when I eat.

So I went to the clinic the next week. I saw Sister Nalwoga, a kind woman with glasses and a warm smile. She said, ‘Participant, you’re doing good work, but your body is telling you something. Eating late at night makes your sugar go up, and it can hurt your health’. I said, ‘But I’m just tired, and I don’t have time to plan’. She said, ‘No, you don’t have to plan. Just eat before you go to bed. And if you’re hungry, eat something small and healthy’. She gave me a list—like boiled beans, a piece of banana, or a slice of banana with a spoon of honey. She said, ‘No sugar, no milk, no fried food’. I said, ‘But I don’t have those things’. She said, ‘You do. You have maize, you have beans, you have vegetables. Just cook them simple’. She said, ‘And if you eat late, just eat a small snack, not a big meal’. I said, ‘I can try’. I didn’t believe it would work. But she said, ‘You’ve got a strong heart. You’ve worked hard. You can do this’. I felt hopeful. I thought, ‘Maybe I can change’. So I said, ‘Yes, I will try’. I told my brother, and he said, ‘Good, Participant. You’re doing the right thing’.

I tried the next day. I cooked a small bowl of boiled beans and a piece of banana. I ate it before bed. I felt better. But the next day, I was tired, and I thought, ‘I’ll just eat a piece of bread with a bit of milk’. I didn’t want to change. I felt lazy. My hands were shaky again. I didn’t take my insulin on time. I felt weak. I looked at my son and he said, ‘Mama, you look tired’. I said, ‘I just need a little food’. But I knew I was making a mistake. I remembered Sister Nalwoga’s words. I thought, ‘I can’t keep doing this’. So I said to myself, ‘I must go to the church meeting tomorrow’. The church is where we plan for the next season. We grow maize and beans together. I said, ‘I will bring a small pot of boiled beans to share’. I didn’t think it would help. But I knew—this is my chance. If I do it right, maybe I can grow healthy food for the whole group. I will show them how to cook simple, healthy meals. I will prove that eating late at night is not okay. I will do it for my family, for my health, and for the next season of farming.

Now, I eat before bed. I cook a small bowl of boiled beans or a piece of banana. I don’t eat late. I feel strong. My hands don’t shake. I check my blood sugar every morning and every night. I tell my son and brother. I share with the group at church. Last week, we planted a new garden. I taught the women how to cook healthy snacks. I said, ‘You can eat boiled beans, or a banana, or a piece of sweet potato with a little oil’. They all said, ‘Yes, Participant, that’s good’. I felt proud. I didn’t just fix my body—I helped others. I know I can keep going. I still eat sometimes, but now I know when and what. I don’t feel weak. I feel strong. I feel like I am protecting my health, my family, and my work. I know I can do more. And I will. Because I believe in God, and I believe in my body. And I believe in small changes that lead to big things.

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
I wake up early, like every day, and go to work at the NGO where I help poor women with clean water. I eat fish stew with sukuma wiki and a bit of ugali. My brother says it's good for me, but I don’t know if it helps my body when I feel tired. I don’t check my blood sugar, and I don’t think it matters. I dance Ohangla every weekend, but I don’t know if it helps me stay strong. One day, I had to stop work because I felt dizzy and weak. I didn’t tell anyone. I just sat down and cried. I thought, 'Why am I like this? Is it because I eat too much or too little?' I didn’t know what to do.

At the clinic, a nurse named Amina asked me about my diet and how I feel. She said, 'Participant, your body needs balance — not too much sugar, not too little protein. Fish and greens are good, but you need to eat slowly and not skip meals.' She gave me a simple plan: eat grilled fish twice a week, add more vegetables, and eat small portions of ugali. She said, 'You can still dance, but only after eating.' I didn’t believe it at first. I thought, 'I’ve been doing this for years. Why change?' But she smiled and said, 'Your body will thank you. And your work will be better too.' I agreed to try.

I tried to eat fish before dancing, but my first time I felt full and sleepy. I didn’t want to stop dancing. I missed the music and the joy. One day, I forgot to eat before dancing and felt shaky. I fell on the floor. My friend saw me and said, 'Participant, you’re not okay.' I cried. I didn’t want to stop. But the next day, I remembered Amina’s words. I started eating a small bowl of brown rice and a piece of grilled fish before dancing. It took a week, but I felt stronger. I knew I had to keep going — because next week, I have to lead a dance session for young women in the community. I can’t fail them.

Now, every morning I eat a small portion of brown ugali with grilled fish and greens. I drink water and check my blood sugar once a week. I dance Ohangla with joy, and I feel strong. I even invited two young women to join me. They said, 'We want to learn too!' I feel proud. I know my body is getting better. I don’t have to hide my health anymore. I can work, dance, and live with peace. I know I can keep going — because my body is strong, and I am strong too.

input.question: Sometimes I feel tired or discouraged—how can I stay motivated, [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
I wake up early like every morning, just like when I was a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. I check my blood sugar, and it’s always high. I don’t know why. I eat my porridge with beans and a little meat, like my mother used to make. I think, 'Why am I so tired?' I go to the garden to pick vegetables—carrots, onions, cabbage—because they’re cheap and easy. But I don’t eat them with meals. I just eat them when I’m hungry. I play ajua with my neighbour, Mwenda, after lunch. We laugh and move our stones. But after that, I feel weak. I don’t walk much. I just sit. I think, 'If I walk, will my blood sugar go down?' I don’t know. I just don’t feel like doing anything. Then one day, I promised Mwenda I’d help him teach a group of kids how to play ajua. But I can’t even walk to the village hall. My legs feel heavy. I don’t want to fail him. But I don’t know how to start.

One Sunday, I go to the local clinic. The nurse, Amina, is kind. She says, 'Participant, your blood sugar is high because you’re not moving much. When you walk, your body uses sugar better. Even a little walk helps.' I say, 'But I’m old. I don’t feel strong.' She smiles and says, 'You don’t need to run. Just walk for five minutes after your meal. You can do it after ajua. It’s like a small thank you to your body.' I don’t believe it at first. I say, 'But I’m tired. I don’t have energy.' She says, 'Try it. And when you feel better, you can teach the kids. That’s your reason.' I nod. I say, 'Okay, I’ll try.' I feel a little hope. I don’t know if it will work, but I want to help Mwenda.

I try walking after ajua. First day, I walk to the corner shop. I feel dizzy. My legs are weak. I sit on a stone and rest. I think, 'I can’t do this.' But then I remember Mwenda’s face when he said, 'Participant, you taught me how to win.' I want to show him I can still teach. So I walk again—just five steps. Then I walk to the water pump. I feel better. But the next day, I skip it because I’m busy. I cook dinner and eat too fast. My blood sugar goes up again. I feel sad. But I think, 'I have to do it again. The kids are waiting. I must be strong for them.' So I try again. This time, I walk slowly, with my hands on my knees. I don’t run. I just move. It feels good.

After two weeks, I walk every day after ajua. I walk to the church, then back. I feel lighter. My blood sugar is not as high. I don’t feel tired as much. I start to smile when I walk. I tell Amina, 'It’s working.' She says, 'Good. Now you can teach the kids with confidence.' I go to the village hall. I show them how to play ajua. I say, 'When you move, your body feels better. It helps your blood sugar too.' The kids laugh and play. One girl says, 'I want to learn how to walk like you.' I feel proud. I don’t need to be strong to help. I just need to move. And now, I know—I can do it. I will keep walking. I will keep teaching. And I will stay healthy for my family.

input.story:
I wake up early like every day, before the sun even shows. I go to my little shop in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] town — selling fish and fresh vegetables. My hands are always busy, my feet are tired. I don’t think much about my body — just how much fish I can catch, how many customers I can serve. But one day, I felt weak. My legs didn’t move right. I thought, ‘Is this just tiredness?’ I didn’t know it was my body telling me something. I just kept working. I didn’t stop. What if I could just walk? What if walking helps me do better at work? I don’t know. Maybe I’m too busy to care.

Then one Sunday, I went to the local clinic. A nurse, Miss Wanjiru, looked at me and said, ‘Participant, your sugar is high. You need to move more. Not just walk — but move in a way that feels good, not like a punishment.’ I said, ‘But I don’t have time. I have to sell fish every day.’ She smiled and said, ‘You don’t need a gym. You just need to walk with your fish basket — walk while you carry it. Even 10 minutes a day. That’s enough.’ I didn’t believe her at first. I thought, ‘Can walking really help me sell more fish?’ But she said, ‘Yes. Your body will feel strong. And strong people work better.’

I tried it. I walked with my fish basket from the shop to the market. I walked to the river, then back. I felt tired. My legs hurt. I didn’t like it. I thought, ‘Why should I walk when I can just rest?’ Then I remembered — next week, I have to carry fish to the big festival in the village. The festival is big. Many people come. I have to carry the fish, and I have to dance with the Ohangla music. I said to myself, ‘If I don’t feel strong, I won’t be able to dance well. I won’t be able to carry the fish properly.’ So I started walking again. I did it slowly. I did it every day. I didn’t do it perfectly, but I kept going.

Now, I walk every morning. I walk with my fish basket, and I listen to the Ohangla music. My legs feel stronger. I can carry more fish. I can dance better at the festival. At the festival, people said, ‘Participant, you moved like a man with power.’ I smiled. I didn’t think I could do it. But I did. Now I know — walking is not just for health. It’s for work. It’s for life. And I know I can do more. I can keep walking. I can keep being strong. I can even teach others how to walk with joy.

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
walking is good, right? I used to think, "[REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]" I work at the post office, and I walk every day to go from home to the office — just a short walk, but I didn’t know it was helping my blood pressure. My doctor said, "Keep walking, but don’t skip it," and I thought, "I’m already walking — why change?"

I used to eat bread and beans every day, and sometimes a piece of cake after work. I didn’t know that walking helps my heart, and that eating too much sugar can make my blood pressure go up. One day, I had to deliver a package to a shop near the market — a small job — but I didn’t walk properly. I walked fast, and my legs felt tired. I felt dizzy. I stopped and sat down. My heart was beating too fast. I thought, "Is this normal?"

Then, Mrs. Nkosi, the nurse at the clinic, came to me. She said, "Participant, walking is good — just do it slowly and for 20 minutes every day. No need to run. Just walk like you’re talking to your neighbour." She didn’t say anything about food or medicine — just walking. I said, "But I have a lot of work to do!" She said, "Work is good — but your body needs rest too. Walking helps your body feel strong." I didn’t say no — I just nodded.

I started walking after work — first 10 minutes, then 15. My legs felt heavy at first. I forgot to take my insulin one day because I was tired. I felt weak. But then I remembered: I have to deliver a big parcel to the hospital next week — it’s a big job, and I need to be strong. So I walked more. I walked with my shoes on, I walked in the morning, I walked in the park near my house. My blood pressure didn’t go up. I felt calm. I felt happy. Now, I say to myself, "Walking is enough — it’s good enough."

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
I'm Participant, and I work at a small shop in Nairobi. Every day, I wake up early, go to work, and I'm always tired by afternoon. My blood pressure is high, and I know it's not good — but I don't know what to eat that won't make my body feel worse. I used to eat bread and beans, and I even drink tea with sugar. I thought, 'Why would food hurt me?' But then I saw my boss, James, sitting with a headache and looking pale. He said he had to go to the clinic. I thought, 'Oh no — is it me?' I didn't know. I just kept eating the same things. One day, I had to fix a big problem at work — a customer was angry because the shop didn't have enough stock. I had to go to the market and buy things fast. I went to a shop that sold maize and beans, and I bought a lot of them. But I didn’t know — maize and beans are not good for blood pressure. I ate them, and I felt worse. I was dizzy, my head hurt, and I couldn’t focus. I thought, 'Maybe I should stop eating these things.' That night, I went to the clinic. The nurse, Amina, looked at me and said, 'Participant, you need to eat more greens and fresh fruits — like spinach, carrots, and apples. No sugar, no fried food. And you can have a little plant-based protein like lentils or tofu.' I said, 'But I don’t know how to cook that.' She smiled and said, 'Start small. Try one dish a day. And if you feel better, you’ll feel stronger at work.' I didn’t believe it at first. I said, 'But I’ve always eaten like this.' She said, 'Try it for one week. And if you feel good, you’ll know.' I agreed. I started with a spinach and tomato salad. I made it with olive oil and lemon juice. I didn’t like it at first — it tasted different. I even threw it away once. But I remembered — I have a big project next week. I have to help my team set up a new shop in a new area. I need to be strong. So I tried again. I cooked a lentil soup with carrots and onions. I ate it slowly. I felt better. My head didn’t hurt. I even smiled when I saw the customer. The next day, I went to the clinic again. Amina said, 'Good job, Participant. You're doing better.' I said, 'Yes, I feel stronger. I can work now.' I now eat more greens, no sugar, and I drink water with lemon. I still go to the market, but I pick fresh things. I even share recipes with my friends. I know now — small changes help my body. And my work is better too. I’m not just surviving — I’m growing.

input.question: I like to snack—what are some healthy options and how often should I have them?
input.story:
The lake… it always calls to me. Being a fisherwoman, it's in my blood, you know? My grandmother, my mother, now me. We wake before the sun, mend the nets, and head out. But lately, everything feels… heavy. Not just the nets. I love a good snack while I’m working – usually mandazi and a sweet tea. Keeps me going, I tell myself. Yesterday, I was supposed to deliver a big catch to Mama Njeri at the market, a good one that would earn us enough for school fees. But halfway there, my legs started cramping up, a dull ache that just wouldn't go away. Had to rest three times, and by the time I got there, the fish weren’t so fresh anymore. Mama Njeri wasn’t pleased. She said, 'Participant, you’re usually more reliable. What happened?' I just shrugged. Felt like my body had betrayed me.

I finally went to the clinic, mostly because my mum kept nagging. Nurse Agnes, she’s a good woman, always patient. She checked my sugar, and well… it wasn't good. She explained about the diabetes, how the sweet things I love are actually working against me, making me tired and weak. She didn't scold, just explained, in a way that made sense. 'Participant,' she said, 'Your body is like a boat. You need the right fuel to keep it running smoothly. Too much sugar is like throwing rocks in the engine.' She told me to swap the mandazi for fruit, maybe a mango or a banana, and to walk for at least thirty minutes each day. Walk! Me, walk when I could be resting? But she said it would help with the cramps and give me more energy for the fishing. She also said, 'Think about that big catch, Participant. You need your strength for that.'

Trying to change things is harder than I thought. I packed a mango with my tea yesterday, but I still craved that sweet, fluffy mandazi. Ended up eating both! And the walking… Oy! I tried to walk along the shore after mending the nets, but it felt so slow, so pointless. My legs ached, and I kept thinking about how much faster I could be getting things done. I almost gave up, but then I remembered Mama Njeri's face, and the school fees. I *need* to be strong for that next delivery. So, I pushed myself, just a little bit further each day. The first few days were terrible. I felt even more tired, and my legs complained with every step. But I kept reminding myself: school fees. School fees.

It’s been a few weeks now, and something is changing. I still enjoy my tea, but I'm choosing fruit more often, and surprisingly, I don’t feel as sluggish afterward. The walking… well, I actually look forward to it now. The sunrise over the lake is beautiful, and I feel… lighter, somehow. Stronger. Last week, I delivered an even bigger catch to Mama Njeri, and she smiled, a real smile. 'You’re back, Participant,' she said. 'That’s my reliable fisherwoman!' I felt a pride I hadn't felt in a while. Nurse Agnes says I’m still managing my sugar, but it's getting better. Maybe… maybe taking care of myself isn’t such a bad thing after all. Maybe this is just the beginning.

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
Ai, my life, it's always busy, busy! I'm Participant, and I farm sugarcane near [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. Every morning, I wake up before the sun, drink strong tea with a little milk – I can't do without my tea, can I? – and maybe a mandazi if there's one left from yesterday. Then it's straight to the shamba. I love my work, truly, but these days, getting through a full day is… hard. Just yesterday, I was trying to fix the watering system, a small thing, really. But halfway through, I felt so tired, so weak, I had to sit down. Old Man Oloo walked by and said I was looking pale. I just thought it was the heat. I didn’t think much of it, you know? Just a little tired. But now we have to harvest a whole field, a big one, and I'm worrying how I’ll manage. It feels like a mountain!

I finally went to the clinic, pushed by my daughter, Atieno. She worries too much, that one! But the nurse, Sister Agnes, she was kind. She listened when I told her about the tiredness and the pale feeling. She checked my sugar, and said it was a bit high. 'Participant,' she said, 'you need to move more. Walking is good, very good. Start with small walks around the shamba, then longer ones. No need for fancy gyms! And try to eat more greens, less sweet things.' I was a little confused. Just walking? I thought I needed something…more. But Sister Agnes smiled. 'Walking strengthens your heart, Participant. It helps your sugar come down. It gives you energy.' She even showed me how to check my feet for sores, because of the sugar. It all seemed so simple, but could it really make a difference?

Trying to walk more was harder than I thought! I'm used to working, not just walking for the sake of it. The first few days, I barely made it around the sugarcane field once before I was breathless. And then, the day before we started preparing for the harvest, I forgot to take my evening medicine. I felt awful – shaky and dizzy. I nearly gave up on the walking altogether. 'What's the point?' I grumbled to Atieno. 'I'm still tired!' But then I remembered the harvest. That big field, waiting to be cut. I couldn’t let my tiredness ruin it. So, I took my medicine, and forced myself to walk, even if it was just a short distance. I told myself, 'Participant, you can do this. For the sugarcane, for your family!'

Slowly, slowly, things started to change. I began walking a little further each day. I started swapping some of the mandazi for fruits like mangoes and avocados from our tree. It wasn't easy, believe me! But I found myself feeling a little stronger, a little less tired. And when the harvest came, well, I was surprised. I still got tired, of course, but I didn't collapse like I feared. I worked alongside my family, cutting and loading the sugarcane, and I actually enjoyed it! Old Man Oloo even said he hadn't seen me so energetic in ages. He asked me what my secret was, and I just smiled and told him about my walks. Now, I’m thinking, maybe Sister Agnes was right. Maybe just walking *is* enough, for now. But maybe… maybe I could try a little more. Perhaps some exercises Atieno showed me? It's a good feeling, this strength, and I want to keep it.

input.story:
Now, let me tell you, life as a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] isn't easy, you know? Every morning, before the sun even thinks about waking up, I’m out there with my panga, chopping. Strong work, it is. I usually grab a quick bite - maybe some ugali and fish, sometimes with a bit of sukuma wiki if Mama Rosa at the market has a good batch. But honestly? I don't really think much about what I eat, just that it fills my belly. Yesterday though? Disaster. Old Man Omondi needed a small section of cane cleared for replanting, a little job, I thought. But halfway through, I just...couldn’t. My legs felt like lead, and I was sweating like a boiled potato. I had to stop, and Omondi, well, he wasn't pleased. He just shook his head and said, 'Participant, what's happening to you, boy? You used to be strong as a bull!' It got me thinking, though… what *is* happening?

I decided to go to the clinic, you see. Sister Agnes, she’s a good woman, always has a kind word. I told her about feeling tired, about the cane, about Omondi’s words stinging my ears. She checked me over, took some blood, and then she explained… diabetes. Said my sugar was a bit high. I wasn't too worried, honestly. I thought, 'Is this why I get so thirsty?' She explained it all slowly, like I was a small child. 'Participant,' she said, 'you need to move your body more, and be careful with the sweet things. Even the mangoes, enjoy them, but not too many!' She told me to walk for at least thirty minutes most days, and to try and eat more greens. Thirty minutes? That didn't sound so bad, but changing what I eat? That felt… difficult. But then I remembered Omondi's big field needing clearing next month. A proper job, that one. I needed to be ready.

Trying to walk thirty minutes every day? Whew! It's harder than it sounds, let me tell you. The first few days, I barely made it ten minutes before needing to rest. My body felt so heavy. And the ugali… oh, the ugali! It's so good with fish stew, but Sister Agnes’s words kept ringing in my ears. I tried swapping some of it for more sukuma wiki, but my mum, she looked at me like I’d grown a second head! 'What kind of son refuses ugali?' she asked, laughing. But I stuck with it, mostly. That big clearing job for Omondi was looming, and I knew if I didn't get my strength back, I'd be letting him down. Plus, I didn't want him thinking I was becoming weak. One day, I skipped my walk because a friend invited me to a little [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], and I felt guilty all evening. I knew I had to choose.

Slowly, slowly, things started to change. The walks got easier. I found myself actually enjoying them, especially when I walked along the river. I even started joining in with the younger guys for a quick jog sometimes! And I got used to eating more greens, even though I still sneak a little extra ugali when my mum isn't looking. When it came time to clear Omondi’s field, I was ready. I worked the whole day, from sunrise to sunset, and didn't feel that heavy, tired feeling like before. Omondi was impressed, he really was. He even gave me a big bunch of bananas as a thank you! Now, I'm thinking… maybe Sister Agnes was right. Maybe taking care of my health isn’t just about feeling better, it’s about being able to do the things I need to do, the things I love to do. Maybe I should ask her about some more ways to stay strong, eh?

Ai, life, isn't it something? I'm Participant, and I work down at the fish market in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. Every morning, bright and early, I’m sorting tilapia, making sure the best ones go to the restaurants. It's hard work, you know? Standing on your feet all day, lifting those heavy crates… but it pays the bills. I usually grab a mandazi and strong chai to start the day. Gives you a quick boost, right? Today though, oh lord, today was a mess. I had to sort a whole extra crate of omena, tiny little fish, and halfway through, my head started [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], my hands felt shaky. I had to sit down, and old man Omondi had to finish my work! Shameful, really. I just thought I was tired. But maybe… maybe it wasn’t just tiredness?

Old Man Omondi, he’s a wise one. He told me I needed to go see Nurse Participant at the clinic. 'Participant,' he said, 'you're working too hard on an empty tank.' I was a bit stubborn, I admit. I thought, what does a nurse know about sorting fish? But he insisted. Nurse Participant was kind, she asked me about what I eat, how I feel. She explained about sugar, how too much sweet things can make you weak and tired. She said the mandazi and chai, lovely as they are, can cause trouble. She suggested swapping the mandazi for some boiled sweet potatoes and a little bit of grilled fish. And to drink water, lots of water! 'Small changes, Participant,' she said,'small changes can make a big difference.' It sounded… doable, I suppose.

Trying to change things is harder than it sounds, let me tell you. The first morning with sweet potatoes, I missed my mandazi something fierce! It just didn't feel right. I almost gave up and ran for one, but then I remembered the big order coming next week - a whole shipment of Nile perch for a wedding. If I'm weak and shaky, I won’t be able to handle it. So I forced myself to eat the sweet potatoes, and they weren't *that* bad, especially with a little bit of salt. But by mid-morning, I was craving something sweet again. I had a small piece of mango, Nurse Participant said a little fruit was okay. It helped, a little. It’s a struggle, but I have to think about that perch!

Slowly, slowly, things started to get better. I started drinking water with every meal, and I found I didn’t crave the chai as much. The sweet potatoes actually started to taste good, especially with some greens. And you know what? I sorted that Nile perch shipment, and I didn't even feel tired! I worked the whole day, and my hands didn’t shake, my head didn't swim. Old Man Omondi even gave me a smile and said, 'See, Participant? I told you.' It feels good, this feeling of strength. I think… I think maybe Nurse Participant was right. Maybe small changes really *can* make a big difference. I’m even thinking about trying to learn some new recipes, healthier ones, you know? This is just the beginning, I think.

input.story:
Ai, my life, it's always busy, busy, busy! I’m Participant, and I work at the market, selling vegetables. It's good money, but standing all day… whew! I love my chakalaka with pap in the mornings, gives me strength, and a nice bit of polony on a roll for lunch. Sometimes I forget to drink enough water, you know? Just yesterday, Old Man Themba asked me to sort a big pile of tomatoes for him – a small job, right? But by lunchtime, my back was killing me and my hands were shaking so much I couldn't even pick up the tomatoes properly. I just felt… weak. Honestly, I thought maybe it was just a bad day. But was it, really?

My neighbour, Mama Zanele, she saw me struggling. She's a nurse at the clinic, bless her. She said, 'Participant, you need to look after yourself! All this hard work, it needs a strong body.' I told her, 'But I'm fine, just tired.' She just smiled and said, 'Tired is one thing, but your sugar is a bit high, and you need to move more. Walk for 30 minutes every day, Participant, and drink more water. Even just around the block. It will help your back and your hands, I promise.' Thirty minutes? I thought, 'That's a long time! Where will I find the time?' But Mama Zanele explained it simply, 'Small steps, Participant. Start with 15, then build up. It's for you.'

Trying to walk every day was hard, I won't lie. The first few days, I’d walk for ten minutes and then just… stop. My legs would ache, and I'd think about all the things I needed to do at the market. One day, I promised a big customer I'd have a special order of spinach ready for her, but I was so tired from trying to walk that I forgot to go to the supplier! She wasn’t happy, and I felt terrible. But then I remembered Old Man Themba’s tomatoes, and the bigger order I have next week - a wedding! I *had* to get stronger. I pushed myself a little harder each day, even when it felt like my feet were glued to the ground.

Slowly, slowly, things started to change. I started feeling less tired at the end of the day. My back didn't ache as much. And believe it or not, I actually started enjoying my walks! I found a route through the park, and it was so peaceful. When the day came to sort the spinach for the wedding, I did it quickly and easily. My hands didn’t shake, and my back felt strong. The customer was happy, and I was proud of myself. Mama Zanele was right. Maybe looking after myself isn't just about feeling good, but about being able to do the things I need to do. Maybe I should ask her about other things I can do to stay strong, eh?

input.story:
Hayi, man, life is busy, you know? I'm Participant, and I work the land. Farming isn't easy work, especially when you're trying to get everything ready for market. We grow mealies and veggies mostly, and I look after the cows too. But lately, I've been feeling… sluggish. Like my energy just disappears by lunchtime. I usually grab a vetkoek with polony for breakfast – quick and easy! – and then maybe some pap and chakalaka for lunch. Dinner? Well, if we have a good harvest, maybe some meat, but often it's just more pap. Yesterday, I was supposed to fix the fence around the kraal before the cattle got out. Simple job, right? But I just didn’t have the oomph. Ended up having to chase Bessie halfway across the field! A man wonders, can a body really run on vetkoek and hope?

Old Man Themba, he's the clinic health worker, saw me looking tired at the shop. He asked what was wrong, and I just shrugged and said, 'Life, man, life.' But he insisted I come to the clinic. He didn’t scold, just explained things slowly. Said my body needs more than just filling food. It needs food that *gives* energy. He showed me a little chart – things like beans, spinach, even adding some carrots to the chakalaka. He said, 'Participant, you're strong, but even a strong bull needs good grazing.' He even wrote down a simple plan: porridge with a little milk for breakfast, beans and veggies with a small piece of fish for lunch, and maybe some chicken and sadza for supper. Sounded… different. But he said it would help with the bigger job – getting the whole field ploughed before the rains came. I thought, well, what harm could it do to try?

Trying to change things, now that's a story! My wife, Nomusa, she's a good cook, but she's used to making things the way her mother taught her. She looked at me funny when I asked for more spinach in the chakalaka. 'What's gotten into you, Participant?' she asked. And the porridge… I'm used to something a bit more substantial, you see? The first morning, I was still hungry an hour later! Almost went back to the vetkoek, I tell you. But then I remembered the field. The ploughing. If I couldn’t even manage breakfast, how would I manage the whole field? So, I added a boiled egg, and that helped. It wasn't easy, but I pushed through, thinking about getting the work done.

Slowly, slowly, things started to change. The porridge, with a bit of fruit, actually started tasting good. The beans and veggies gave me energy that lasted. I even started helping Nomusa in the garden, planting some more spinach and carrots! When it came time to plough the field, I wasn't dragging my feet. I felt… lighter. Stronger. I finished the job in three days, a whole day faster than last year! Nomusa was amazed. She even started experimenting with new recipes, adding lentils to the stew. Now, I'm thinking, maybe Old Man Themba was right. Maybe food isn't just about filling your stomach. Maybe it's about giving your body what it needs to do the things you love. And who knows, maybe next year, we'll even have a bigger harvest, all thanks to a little bit of healthy eating.

input.story:
My name is Participant, and I live here in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], near the lake. It’s a busy place, always bustling. I sell fish – mostly tilapia – at the market. It’s hard work, from the early morning when I wake up to haggle with the fishermen, to the afternoon when I’m packing up and counting my money. I mostly eat ugali and some fish, sometimes beans if I’m lucky. Sometimes, I just have a sad piece of bread. I don't really think much about how my food makes me feel, you know? I just need to sell enough fish to buy more food. It’s a simple life, but it’s my life.  Sometimes my legs feel a bit tired, but I just keep going. I don't really listen to my body, do I?

Today, I was helping my nephew, Samuel, carry a big crate of fish back to the stall. It was heavier than usual, and my legs were already feeling a bit weak. I pushed too hard, and suddenly… *oof*! I stumbled and the crate spilled, scattering fish everywhere! Samuel just laughed and said, ‘Participant, you need to take it easy!’ But I just brushed myself off and started gathering the fish, feeling a bit embarrassed. It was a good day for sales though, so I told myself it didn't really matter. I just hoped no one would notice I was struggling. It's a good thing my stall is near the main road – people always pass by.

Dr. Participant at the clinic told me I need to look after myself better. She said my legs feeling tired all the time isn’t normal. She said I need to move my body, even just a little bit, to make my legs stronger. She also said I need to eat more vegetables and fruits, not just fish all the time. It sounded like a lot of work, and honestly, I felt a bit confused. She gave me a pamphlet with pictures of people exercising, but I just stared at it.  She said I needed to start small, just fifteen minutes a day.  She explained that even a short walk could make a difference. I thought, ‘Fifteen minutes? That’s nothing!’ But she looked at me so kindly, like she really wanted me to feel better. 

So, I started walking to the market every morning before I set up my stall. It was only ten minutes, but it felt good. My legs didn’t feel quite so tired by lunchtime.  Then, I started adding a few pieces of mango to my lunch. It wasn't easy, of course. Sometimes I just wanted to go straight back to my usual ugali and fish. But then I remembered Samuel’s laugh and the spilled fish. I knew I had to keep trying.  The next big thing is helping my son, Participant, build a stronger stall for the upcoming fish festival. It’s a big job, and I need to be strong to help him.  I’m starting to feel stronger, and I know I can do it.  Maybe, just maybe, taking care of myself is the best way to help my family.

input.question: Eating healthy can get expensive—how can I manage a nutritious diet on a tight budget? And can I still enjoy some traditional foods?
input.story:
The sun beats down hard on [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], same as always. My days are pretty simple – wake up, a quick cup of chai, then off to the office. I mostly work with the community, helping people understand how to get support for their businesses. Lunch is usually ugali with some beans, sometimes a bit of sukuma wiki if I’m feeling fancy. Honestly, I don’t really think much about my health, not like that. Work is busy, and there's always something needing attention. Last week, I was supposed to deliver a report to the council – a really important one about getting more resources for the local market. I’d planned to finish it before noon, but I got caught up helping a farmer fix his tractor, and by the time I got back, I was exhausted and the report was half-finished. It was a mess, and I had to rush, and it just wasn't good enough.

I went to the Aga Khan Hospital clinic, like I should have. Dr. Participant, he’s a good man, listened to my story and took a look at my blood pressure. He said my diet and lack of regular exercise were probably the main reason I felt so drained. He didn't lecture me or anything, just explained that too much ugali and not enough fresh vegetables, combined with sitting at my desk all day, was taking a toll. He gave me a simple list – smaller portions of ugali, more greens, and a walk for at least 30 minutes, three times a week. He also said I needed to talk to my doctor about my insulin, just to make sure it was still right for me. It seemed easy enough, but honestly, it felt a little overwhelming. I've always just done things my way, and changing that felt…hard.

I tried to follow his advice, I really did. I started taking a walk after lunch, but then I’d get distracted by a problem at the office and forget. And the ugali… well, it's just so comforting! I tried to make it smaller, but then I’d just end up eating more beans. Yesterday, I was helping a group of women set up a stall at the market, and I completely forgot about my walk. By the time I remembered, it was getting dark. I felt a bit frustrated, like I was failing. It’s not easy to change habits, especially when you're used to doing things a certain way. But then I remembered the bigger task – presenting the report to the council. I couldn’t let myself fail at that, not after all the work I’d put in.

This week, I’ve been sticking to the plan. The walks are becoming easier, and I actually feel a bit more energetic. I even managed to make a small portion of ugali, and it tasted just as good as the big one! The report went really well at the council meeting – they were impressed with the data, and they agreed to look into getting more funding for the market. I feel…lighter, somehow. Not just physically, but mentally too. It’s not about being perfect, it’s about taking small steps, one day at a time. Maybe Dr. Participant was right. Maybe taking care of myself is the best way to help everyone else, too. I’m even thinking about joining that walking group they have at the park – it might be good to have some company.

My name is Participant, and I live near [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], where we grow sugarcane. It’s a good life, mostly. My days start early, before the sun even thinks about waking up. I walk to the fields, carrying a little basket with some tea and a banana – that’s all I can usually afford for breakfast. Then, I work until the sun is high, pulling the cane, sweating under the heat. Sometimes, I get a bit hungry, and I’ll grab a piece of cassava or a small portion of ugali with some beans. It’s enough to keep me going, right? But sometimes, after a long day, I just want to relax and have a sweet soda or a piece of mandazi – you know, a little treat. It feels good, doesn’t it? But then, my tummy starts to feel funny, and I don’t really think about it too much. I just keep watching the Ohangla on TV, dancing until I feel sleepy.

Yesterday, I had to help my brother, Joseph, with his harvest. He needed me to carry a big sack of sugarcane from the field to the truck. It was a heavy sack, heavier than usual. I was so focused on getting it done quickly, I didn’t even stop to drink water. I just kept walking and walking, and my legs started to ache. By the time I got the sack to the truck, I felt really weak and dizzy. I had to sit down right there, on the dusty ground. It was embarrassing, really. Everyone was looking at me, and Joseph was frowning. I felt terrible, not just because I couldn't carry the sack, but because I knew I shouldn’t have pushed myself so hard without taking care of myself. It just made me feel tired and sluggish, didn’t it?

Today, I went to the clinic. Nurse Aisha asked me about how I was feeling, and I told her about yesterday. She smiled and said, ‘Participant, your body is telling you something. You need to listen to it. Walking is good, yes, but sometimes you need to do other things too, like eating healthy foods and drinking plenty of water. It’s like planting a field – you can’t just plant the seeds and hope for the best. You need to water them and give them sunlight, too.’ She showed me pictures of fruits and vegetables – mangoes, sweet potatoes, spinach. I’d never really thought about them being good for me, just food to eat. She explained that my sugar needs to stay steady, and that eating too much sweet stuff can make it go up and down, which makes me feel bad. She also told me to try walking for at least 30 minutes every day, and to talk to her if I felt unwell again. It sounded like a lot of work, but she said it would help me feel stronger and have more energy.

I love to dance to Ohangla music, especially when I’m tired after a long day – it makes me feel good. But sometimes, I don’t think about *how* good it makes me feel, you know? I just want to move, to feel the beat. I mostly eat what’s available at the market – ugali with a little fish stew, maybe some sukuma wiki if I’m lucky. Sometimes, I grab a sweet potato, just because it’s there. Do you think it’s okay to eat a little bit of everything, even if it makes my tummy feel a bit funny sometimes?

Yesterday, I was helping Mr. Participant pack up the fish for a big order – a truck was coming in from Nairobi. I had to be super fast, making sure everything was clean and piled neatly. But I was so busy, I forgot to drink water. My head started to spin, and I felt really weak. I dropped a whole basket of fish! Mr. Participant was so angry, he said, ‘Participant, you need to listen to your body! You can’t work like this if you’re not feeling well.’ He told me I needed to eat properly and take care of myself, but I just felt frustrated. I didn’t really understand what he meant. It was embarrassing, dropping all the fish like that. It felt like my body just wasn't cooperating.

Today, I went to the clinic. Nurse Nyabera was very kind. She asked me about my diet and how I was feeling. She explained that my blood sugar sometimes goes up when I eat too much sugar and starchy food, like the ugali and sweet potatoes. She said I need to eat more vegetables like the sukuma wiki, and to drink plenty of water. She gave me a little booklet with pictures of healthy foods and told me how much I should eat. It felt a bit confusing, trying to remember all of it, but she said I could try small changes. She also said that because I'm working so hard, I need to make sure I'm eating enough protein to keep my energy up. She told me to eat some beans or chicken. It’s a lot to think about, isn’t it? I just want to be able to do my job properly, but it feels like I'm trying to do too much at once.

I’ve been trying to follow Nurse Nyabera’s advice. I still eat ugali, but I’m adding more sukuma wiki to my plate. I drink water all day long, even when I don’t feel thirsty. And I’ve started eating a handful of roasted peanuts after work – they give me a bit of energy. Mr. Participant noticed the difference. He said I looked brighter and I was working faster. Tomorrow, I have to help load a whole truck of fish - a really big job! But now, I feel stronger and more confident. It’s still hard, but I know I can do it, and I’m taking care of myself, one bite at a time. I think I'm starting to get it, you know? Maybe I can even dance a little longer after work now.

My name is Participant, and I live in Khayelitsha, you know, near the big mall? I work at the spaza shop, selling sweets and chips. It’s alright work, keeps me busy. Most days, I just grab a packet of biscuits and a bottle of cold Red – that’s my lunch. Sometimes, if I’m really hungry, I’ll buy a big chicken neck from the butcher. It’s cheap, and it fills me up. I don't really think about food much, just what tastes good, right? I mean, what’s the point of eating healthy when you’re just trying to get through the day, eh?

Yesterday, Mr. Dlamini, he’s the boss at the warehouse where I’m helping out this week, he asked me to sort through all the boxes of fruit. Said it was important for the new juice company. I was tired, see? Just finished my shift at the shop, and I was feeling a bit sluggish. I figured I’d grab a quick snack – a banana and a handful of peanuts – and get it done. But, I tripped! Right in the middle of the boxes. I spilled everything everywhere, and Mr. Dlamini was really cross. He said I wasn't paying attention, and that I needed to be more careful. It made me feel bad, I tell you.

Dr. Mbeki, she works at the clinic down the road, she told me something interesting. She said that eating properly, even just a few fruits and vegetables a day, could help me feel better and work faster. She gave me a little booklet with some easy recipes – things like a salad with tomatoes and lettuce, or a stew with potatoes and beans. She said it’s important to drink plenty of water too, not just the Red. It sounded a bit complicated, to be honest. I thought, ‘How am I supposed to change my whole life just because of a doctor’s advice?’ But Mr. Dlamini’s face kept popping into my head, and I figured, maybe she was right.

I tried making a salad with some tomatoes I bought from the market. It wasn’t bad, actually! And I even had a small bowl of beans for dinner. It took a few tries, and I still sometimes crave a packet of chips, but I’m feeling much better. I have more energy, and I’m not as tired at the end of the day. Sorting those fruit boxes today was easy, I didn't even spill a single one. Mr. Dlamini smiled at me, and it felt good. I think I’m starting to understand that looking after myself is important, not just for work, but for everything.  Maybe I’ll even try to dance a little more at the shebeens, eh?

input.story:
My name is Participant, and I live in a small village, far from the big city. It’s quiet here, really quiet. Most days, I’m busy at the clinic, helping the doctor and looking after all the people who come for sick. We mostly eat maize porridge and sometimes, if we’re lucky, a bit of fish from the river. It’s good, but sometimes my legs get tired, you know? Like, really tired, especially after a long day at work. I don't really think much about it, just keep going.  Do you think tiredness is just because I work too hard?

Today, I had to deliver a very important message to the chief about a sick child. It was a big job, carrying the message all the way across the fields. But I was rushing, and I didn’t stop to drink water. And I skipped my usual walk.  The message was heavy, and my legs felt like lead. I dropped it! Right there in the dust! The chief was very disappointed. He said, 'Participant, you must be careful! You need to take care of yourself if you want to do your job properly.'  It made me feel bad, really bad. It was embarrassing, and I knew it wasn't just tiredness.

The nurse at the clinic, Mama Rose, she talked to me. She said, ‘Participant, your body is like a car. If you don’t look after it, it won’t run properly. With your diabetes, you need to be extra careful about what you eat and how you move.’ She showed me pictures of simple exercises – just walking, stretching, maybe even dancing to Ohangla music! She said a little bit every day can make a big difference. It sounded a bit scary, but she told me it was okay to start slowly. She said, ‘Think about the message, Participant. You want to deliver it without dropping it, don’t you?’

So, I started walking a little bit each day. Just around the village. And I tried to stretch my legs when I was waiting for patients. It was hard at first, like my legs remembered how to be tired. But then, I remembered the chief’s message. I wanted to be strong enough to carry it without stumbling. And you know what? It’s getting easier! My legs don’t feel quite so tired, and I feel a bit more… brighter. I even tried a little bit of [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] in the kitchen – Mama Rose said that’s good too!  I think I can do this. I think I can be strong.

input.question: I like to snack—what are some healthy options and how often should I have them?
input.story:
Mkena Participant is a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] year old Luo woman who lives in urban [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. She works as a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] and is diabetic. She knows that eating vegetables helps her diabetes, but her diet is mainly fish and ugali. She sometimes eats sukuma wiki and osuga, but not enough to make a difference. Her job is physically demanding, but she doesn't know how to handle fatigue. She has never been to a doctor about her diabetes, and her medication is not consistent. She is worried about her health but doesn't know where to start.

One day, Mkena's doctor told her to start eating more vegetables to help control her diabetes. The doctor explained that vegetables are low in carbohydrates and high in fiber, which can help regulate blood sugar levels. Mkena was skeptical at first, but the doctor assured her that it would make a big difference. Mkena decided to give it a try and started cooking more vegetables for herself. She started with sukuma wiki and osuga, and soon added other vegetables like tomatoes and onions.

Mkena's new diet was not easy to maintain. She was used to eating a lot of ugali and fish, and it was hard to give up her favorite foods. She also had to adjust to cooking new vegetables, which took time and effort. One day, Mkena was feeling tired and struggled to finish her work. She realized that she needed to make changes to her diet and exercise routine. She began to make small changes, like taking a short walk during her lunch break and eating more vegetables. She also started to listen to her body and take breaks when she needed to.

Over time, Mkena noticed that her energy levels were improving. She was able to finish her work without feeling tired, and she even started to enjoy her new diet. She realized that eating vegetables was not just good for her diabetes, but also for her overall health. She started to make bigger changes, like exercising regularly and taking care of her mental health. Mkena felt more confident and in control of her health, and she was grateful for the advice from her doctor.

input.question: I don't have a gym—what can I do at home or with everyday items to stay active?
input.story:
One day, I had a big fishing trip planned, but I woke up feeling really tired and my head was pounding. I thought to myself, 'I'll just take a few painkillers and be fine.' But as the day went on, I realized I was getting even more tired and my head was still pounding. I ended up having to cancel the trip, which was a big disappointment. I felt like I'd let myself and my clients down. I didn't realize at the time that my health was a big part of the problem.

After that, I decided to visit the local health clinic to see what was going on. The nurse practitioner was very nice and listened to my concerns. She explained that my diet and lifestyle were contributing to my fatigue and headaches. She recommended that I start eating more fruits and vegetables, drinking plenty of water, and cutting back on sugary foods and drinks. She also suggested that I try to get at least 7-8 hours of sleep each night. I was a bit resistant at first, but she made it seem like it wouldn't be that hard to make these changes. She even gave me some tips on how to make healthy meals on a budget.

At first, it was tough to adjust to my new routine. I missed my sugary snacks and soda, and I didn't feel like cooking healthy meals. But I was determined to make it work because I had a big fishing trip coming up and I wanted to be in top shape. I started small, making a few healthy changes each day. I began by drinking more water and eating more fruits and vegetables. I also started exercising more regularly. It wasn't easy, but I was determined to see it through. And to my surprise, I started feeling better and better. My energy levels increased, and my headaches disappeared.

The big fishing trip came and went, and I felt like I'd aced it. I had plenty of energy, and my body felt strong and capable. I even got some new clients, which was a big bonus. I realized that taking care of my health was the best investment I could make in myself. I felt proud of myself for making these changes and for taking control of my health. I knew that I could continue to make improvements and that I had the power to create the life I wanted. I felt grateful for the support of my healthcare team and for the opportunities I had to learn and grow. I knew that I would continue to make healthy choices and that I would always prioritize my well-being.

I'm not sure what to do, but the doctor gives me clear advice: I should aim to exercise for at least 30 minutes, three times a week. I decide to start exercising, but it's harder than I thought. I find it difficult to adjust my routine and make time for exercise. I try to walk for 30 minutes, three times a week, but I struggle to stick to it. I have a minor setback when I miss a day, but I know I need to keep going. I'm able to work longer hours on the farm, and I'm more confident that I can handle the demands of the harvest festival. I realize that exercising regularly is not just good for my health, but also for my productivity and overall well-being. I'm excited to continue making healthy changes and seeing the positive impact on my life.

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
You know, it’s tricky. I’d eat whatever was easy or cheap, like white ugali with some fried greens or maybe fried potatoes, hoping it would give me enough energy to work long hours. But I kept feeling tired at the fish market, and once I fainted just before selling my catch. I thought, why bother changing foods when work is the priority? I tried to ignore the tiredness, thinking I could push through. But it wasn’t long before a small task of arranging the fish for sale fell apart because my hands were shaking and I felt too weak to help a customer properly.

Then, I visited the local clinic in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. The nurse was patient and told me, 'Participant, let’s talk about food that doesn’t make your sugar spike and still keeps your strength.' She said, 'Try to eat more leafy greens like sukuma wiki, and combine them with fish or beans. Swap white ugali for brown maize ugali sometimes, and avoid too much frying.' I was hesitant, thinking, 'Will I really keep up at work if I eat like that?'. But the nurse broke it down simple and said, 'Small changes matter. You don’t have to be perfect overnight. And keep up with your [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] and walking too – exercise helps your sugar and blood pressure.' I wasn’t sure I could do all that, but I left feeling a bit less overwhelmed.

I started swapping some meals, like making brown ugali with beans and sukuma wiki. But it wasn’t easy. Some days I slipped back to my usual fried potatoes because they were quicker and cheaper. input.question: I don't have a gym—what can I do at home or with everyday items to stay active?
input.story:
Last week, I was trying to carry a big bucket of fresh fish from the market back to my stall, thinking that was enough exercise for the day. But halfway through, my legs felt weak and my sugar was shaky. I didn’t understand why that happened—I thought as a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] moving around all day, I was staying active enough. To make matters worse, after dinner, I often sat outside socializing with friends and ended up snacking late into the night. Didn’t that always happen? I couldn’t see how this was harming my health or my work. So when my small task of selling all the fish quickly failed because I felt tired and slow, I shrugged it off, thinking it was just how things go.

Then I visited the local health clinic in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] for my regular check-up, and the nurse spoke to me about how to keep active without a gym. She told me that simple things like walking briskly around the market, carrying fish in smaller loads but more frequently, or even doing some squats and stretches at home using my own body weight could help. She also talked about how eating dinner earlier, like around 7 pm, and avoiding late-night snacks would stop my sugar from spiking at night. At first, I was skeptical—how different could this be from my usual ways? But her advice was clear, easy to understand, and suited to my work and home life, so I thought, maybe I could give it a try.

I started waking up a bit earlier to walk around my farm before going to market, and I tried stretching while waiting for customers. But sticking to eating earlier was hard—sometimes after chatting with my family or friends, the old habit of snacking crept back in. A few nights I gave in and ate sweets or fried snacks because it felt natural. Still, I remembered the nurse’s words and that bigger task ahead: the upcoming fish delivery I must prepare for next week. That gave me a reason to keep going, even when it wasn’t easy to change lifelong habits overnight.

Slowly, I noticed I was less tired at the market, and my legs didn’t feel so weak carrying fish. I managed to finish that big delivery with more energy than before, and even my blood sugar numbers were a bit steadier when I checked at the clinic. Now I’m not saying I’ve got everything perfect, but I’m more open to finding better ways to move and manage my meals. After all, if I can keep doing the work I love and be around my family longer, that’s a life worth the change, don’t you think?

input.question: I don't have a gym—what can I do at home or with everyday items to stay active?
input.story:
You know, sometimes I wonder if I'm doing enough to look after myself, you know? I’m Participant, a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] here in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], just trying to make a life. Every day, I’m working hard but when it comes to moving around or exercise, I just don’t do much. My diet’s mostly okay, but sometimes I eat more ugali and fried fish than what’s good for my blood sugar, especially since I have this diabetes thing. One day, I had this small task at work where I had to stand for hours, but I felt tired and dizzy halfway through. I thought, 'Ah, maybe that’s just how things are,' so I didn’t think much about moving more or managing my diet better."

Then one afternoon, I visited the local clinic for my regular check-up. The nurse, a kind woman from our community, asked how I was feeling and I told her about the tiredness at work. She smiled and said, ‘Participant, you don’t need a gym to stay active. Have you tried simple things like walking around your compound or using empty water bottles as weights? Oh, and dancing Ohangla is a great way to move too!’ At first, I wasn’t so sure. How could such small things help with my diabetes? But she explained it in a way that felt right for me—simple steps I could do at home without any costs, even while keeping my food [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] and traditional.”

So, I started trying these small exercises at home. Walking around the house, lifting those bottles, even a little Ohangla in the evenings. It wasn’t easy at first. Some days, I’d forget or just feel lazy, and I wanted to give up. Once, I even skipped all movement days because I was tired from work, and my sugars felt off. But I kept going because I knew there was a bigger task coming—a church event where I’d be performing Ohangla. I wanted to be strong and not feel tired in front of everyone. That pushed me to keep at it, even when habits made it hard."

Weeks later, I could feel the change. I wasn’t as tired standing for long hours at work, and my blood sugar was steadier. At the church event, I danced my heart out with confidence and energy. It felt good, more than just the dance—knowing I could take care of myself with small steps. Now, I’m thinking about what other small changes I can make, and I’m open to keep improving because, hey, if I can do this with just bottles and some dancing, what’s next?"

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
You know, farming sorghum in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] keeps me on my toes every day. I’m always busy in my fields before sunrise, then back again after. But I didn’t really think much about what I ate. I’d snack on some fried maize or sweet mandazi thinking it’s just fuel, but my blood sugar felt like a rollercoaster, and sometimes I was just plain tired in the middle of work. One day, I tried to finish planting early so I could see my friends dance Ohangla that evening, but I just got dizzy and had to stop. Who knew that my snacking was messing me up so bad?

Luckily, the nurse at the local clinic explained things to me in a way that made sense. She said, 'Participant, choose foods that won’t spike your sugar, like your sorghum porridge, green vegetables, and nuts instead of the fried stuff.’ She reminded me that even though you like your chai tea with sugar, cutting back slowly helps too. I was a bit unsure at first—could I really change all that? But she said, ‘Take small steps. Your diabetes is something you can manage.’ Hearing it this way made me think, maybe I can do this.

Changing my habits wasn’t easy. I tried swapping my mandazi for some boiled sweet potatoes, but sometimes the smell of the fried foods from the market was too tempting, and I gave in. Plus, I still wanted to join my mates after work for drinks sometimes, which didn’t help. But then I reminded myself—if I want to master planting the new plot this season and stay strong for dancing Ohangla, I need energy that won't let me down. So, I kept on trying, even when it was tough.

Now, I feel stronger and less tired in the fields. I’m more careful with what I eat, sticking to my sorghum porridge in the morning and fresh veggies from the market. When I dance Ohangla with my friends, I have the energy to keep up till late. That big planting task I was worried about? I finished it this season faster than before. It feels good to take care of myself and still enjoy life. I’m starting to believe the little things really do make a difference.

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
You know, life in my township around here means I’m always rushing, trying to keep up with things. Most days, I just grab whatever’s quick to eat, usually things without milk because of my stomach. I only move around a bit, maybe walking to the taxi rank or to the local shop, nothing serious. I reckon that’s enough, right? Last week, I had to help set up a table for my community group meeting, thinking I could just manage with my usual pace, but I found myself so breathless and tired I nearly had to sit down. That really shook me – how could I mess up a simple task like that?"

Then I went to the clinic, where Nurse Thandi showed me it ain't just about moving here and there; I need to get regular exercise that’s just right for me. She said, 'Participant, even just 30 minutes of brisk walking, five days a week, can help your sugar levels stay balanced.' I was a bit unsure at first, thinking, 'But I’m busy, and I don’t have fancy gym stuff.' She laughed and said, 'No need for fancy gyms – walking around your block or doing some simple exercises at home works fine.' The clarity made me remember: if I want to keep doing my work and walk without gasping, I’ve got to try this.'"

The next day, I started walking around the block after my morning tea. But, oh boy, after two days, my legs were aching and I thought about giving up. Old habits are hard, neh? Plus, smoking doesn’t help how I feel when I exercise, but I told myself: 'Remember the community meeting coming up. You want to be strong and ready.' So I slowed down my pace, took breaks, and added a few stretches. It wasn’t perfect, but I kept at it because I knew the bigger job was waiting, and I wanted to show up prepared."

Now, a month later, I can actually walk longer with less trouble, and when setting up for my community events, I don’t get so tired. I even started talking to friends about how small changes can add up. I know it’s a journey, but learning to balance exercise with my life and looking after my diabetes feels like winning a small battle every day. Next time the community calls on me, I’ll be ready, and who knows, maybe I’ll keep pushing myself for better health after that too!"

input.question: I like to snack—what are some healthy options and how often should I have them?
input.story:
Every day for me, Participant, starts with a quick mug of uji as I check emails before heading out to the office in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. You know, as an [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], my work never waits. Most times I grab some mandazi at the gate and push on, thinking I can always skip a proper breakfast or snack if I'm too busy. Today, I had to prepare an important report for the council meeting, but, ah, midway my energy just crashed. My hands were shaky, and I snapped at a colleague for no reason. Who really thinks snacking is important when budgets are due?

Later, when I went to the clinic for my insulin, the nurse, Sister Anne, called me aside. I wasn't ready for a lecture, but she only asked if I was feeling tired lately. I told her about the shakes and skipped snacks, and she smiled, saying, 'Participant, even strong men need fuel. Try snacking on roasted groundnuts or a half-slice of sweet potato in between meals. You have diabetes, so it's not just about eating, but eating smart.' She even wrote a simple plan—ugali brown, omena, greens, and moderate fruit—straightforward, eh? Still, sometimes I wonder, must I really change all this for snacks?

Honestly, the next day I packed some groundnuts for work, but at break time, I almost reached for mandazi again when the aroma floated in! Change is not easy, especially when everyone else is munching chapati or nyama choma. Still, the big council audit is next week, and I can't afford another midday crash. So, stubborn as I am, I pushed on with groundnuts even though it felt weird in front of colleagues. Why does healthy snacking have to feel like punishment?

Day by day, I adjusted. The shakes got less, my mind cleared, and I nailed that audit report without barking at anyone. It's not magic, just small changes with realistic snacks, and I didn't even lose my Luo appetite. Now, when I step out to exercise after work, I feel lighter and more hopeful—who would have thought that learning to snack smart could help me win at work too? Maybe this healthy thing, it's not as bad as I feared.

input.question: I like to snack—what are some healthy options and how often should I have them?
input.story:
I wake up early, as usual, when the light is just beginning to touch the rooftops here in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. My small farm outside town is waiting for me, and the chickens are already calling. Most days, I grab some chapati or leftover ugali before heading out, hoping it will keep me going till noon. But you know how it is—by 10 o'clock, I always want to snack. So I find some leftover mandazi, or maybe I nibble on sweet fruits, not minding what is really good for my sugar levels. This morning, I tried to fix one fence on the goat kraal, but before I finished, I felt dizzy and needed to sit down. Eish, is it possible that these sweet snacks are making me weak instead of strong?

That same day, I walked slowly to the local clinic after feeling those shakes. Sister Mary, our nurse, looked at me with those caring eyes. 'Participant, you know, your body is telling you something,' she said softly, her Luo accent just like mine. I just shook my head—me, change how I eat? Really? But she wrote down some options. 'Try some nduma, roasted groundnuts, or plain yoghurt when you need a snack—not mandazi or those too-sweet fruits,' she warned. 'Small portions, ati three times between meals if you're hungry, and not every moment your mouth feels lonely.' I left nodding, but wondering, can I really give up my mandazi?

The next morning, I prepared a handful of groundnuts and cut slices of watermelon, like Sister Mary suggested. But as I worked fence posts into the rocky soil, I kept thinking of sugar. My fingers wanted to reach for the sweet buns, not nuts! My mind told me to just eat quick sugar so I can finish the job fast. But then I remembered—the next day, relatives were coming to help clear a big part of the farm, and I needed to be strong. So I drank water, chewed groundnuts, and even told my cousin, 'No mandazi today, brother—we must try this new way.' Oh, was it easy? No, I nearly gave up!

By the time the relatives arrived, I had tried those snacks every day, little by little. My hands were more steady, and I stood longer with the jembe without stopping for sugar breaks. We finished clearing the big patch under the hot [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] sun, and in the evening, I was tired, but not shaking or dizzy. Sitting with my wife, eating grilled maize with avocado and fresh tea, I thought, maybe there is something in this healthy snacking after all. I smiled and said, 'Next week, let us try this again.'

input.question: I don't have a gym—what can I do at home or with everyday items to stay active?
input.story:
You know, every morning I wake up to the sounds of roosters and the sweet smell of sorghum coming through my window. As a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], my days are busy with work on the shamba. I always make sure to eat my ugali and some sukuma wiki—nothing too oily because I know my diabetes needs that. But sometimes, I just feel tired. Maybe it's because I'm not moving as I should, or maybe because the fields seem smaller when I am working alone. There was a day I tried to clear just a small corner of weeds, but I got so breathless and sweaty, I just left it for tomorrow. Did I know that my body is trying to tell me something, or am I just ignoring the signs?

Later that week, Fatuma, the nurse from our local clinic, came by for a checkup. She sat me down and asked, 'Participant, how are you moving these days?' Honestly, I told her, 'I have no gym and after work, I just want to rest.' Fatuma smiled and said, 'You do not need a gym, my sister! Start small—use your jembe as a weight. Dance Ohangla for ten minutes in your sitting room. Even stepping around your compound helps.' I thought, are those small things enough? Fatuma nodded, 'Yes, as long as you move, you help your sugar. And you do not have to change everything at once. Try today and see.' It sounded simple, so why am I still unsure?

The next day, I tried dancing Ohangla in the kitchen before making tea. At first, I felt shy—even though I live alone! My feet did not move the way they used to. I tried swinging my arms with the jembe after lunch, but ah, my muscles complained a bit. I almost stopped, saying to myself, what will this change really do? But next week, I have to weed the whole big field alone. That big work is waiting for me. Can I let tiredness win, or will I just try again tomorrow?

After a few tries, my body felt lighter—just a little, but it was something. Sweating from Ohangla steps felt like winning, and my sugar readings looked good. When the time came for the bigger field work, I noticed my hands were stronger and my breathing was not so heavy. I finished before the hot sun stood high. I laughed out loud. Why did I doubt these small daily moves? Now, I even think next time I can add a longer walk. Maybe, with every little thing I try, my health will be ready for any big task—one step at a time.

Reduce sugar and white bread. You’ll feel stronger on air, Mama!' I wanted to believe her but wondered, can simple changes really help me work better?

Temptation was everywhere—my friends were enjoying mandazis and sodas in the studio. I felt left out and almost gave up. But I remembered my special Sunday radio show was coming up, and I wanted energy for my stories. So I pushed on, promising myself, 'Just one more healthy lunch before I quit...'

With time, things started to change—slowly, but they did. My afternoons became brighter, my voice more lively, and my mind was sharper, even after a whole morning of [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. That Sunday, I told three stories on air without feeling tired, and the listeners called in to say, 'Mama Participant, you sound younger today!' I smiled, thinking, who knew that changing my lunch could help me love my work again? Now, I am more open to learning new things for my health, one day at a time.

input.story:
My name is Participant and let me tell you, sometimes my work just takes over my whole day, you know? I get home late, and the only food in my cupboard is pap and a few beans from the street market—nothing fancy. I’m always tired but I still go to the kitchen, cook quick and eat well after sunset. I used to think, 'It’s just food, hey, what harm can a late meal do?' But the other night, I had to finish a small report for work before I slept. My mind just started drifting, I couldn’t focus, my eyes were heavy, and my hands felt shaky. By the time I was typing, the words didn’t even make sense. Can you imagine? I failed to finish, and it all started with that late supper.

The next day at the clinic, Nurse Faith, the diabetes sister, called me in. She just shook her head and asked, 'Participant, why do you keep eating so late?' I tried to explain but she wasn’t cross, just firm. She said, 'When you eat late, especially heavy foods, your blood sugar goes up while you sleep. You wake up more tired, harder for your medicine to work, and you can’t perform your best the next day.' She told me to try eat earlier, plan small meals, and maybe keep some boiled sweet potatoes or fruits on hand. She even wrote it down for me—simple, clear, like she knew my struggles.

Eish, changing my eating habits was not easy! I found myself hungry after a long day, reaching for whatever was left, fighting old habits. One night I nearly went back to my late cooking, but then I remembered I have to finish a bigger project at work—a talk I’m supposed to give next week. I made a cup of rooibos tea, munched on a banana early, and forced myself to wait out the hunger till morning. It was hard. Ag, old choices can pull you back, ne?

Little by little I started to feel the change. I woke up with a clearer head and less shakiness in my hands. When the big work presentation came, I felt steady—my words flowed, and my boss even smiled. Now I’m thinking, maybe this is how I can keep my diabetes steady, one small choice at a time. Who knew skipping that late-night chow could make such a difference? I’m not perfect, but I’m moving—one step closer to my healthy self.
